chapter: Early life and New York years
title: Hearing live bands and playing in New York with the Conrad Janis band
summary: He lists Los Angeles bands he heard, then musicians met in New York with Janis's Tailgate Five, Hines in San Francisco, and Muggsy Spanier's influence.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Who else did you hear live other than Horry's band? Who else did you hear? Who else did you hear?

In Los Angeles in those days, there was a guy named Pete Daly out of Chicago-style Dixieland band. He was quite good. Clareness, Rosie McHarg. It's a long time since I really thought about those people. I never was fond of playing that way. I found myself in New York in the 50s, 50 to 55, playing alongside an incredible roster of musicians. This was in the days with the Conrad Janus band. Conrad Janus on the Tailgate Five, he called it. It was a five-piece group usually. But we'd play alongside just about the who's who of jazz, really. We'd see Henry Red Allen all the time, Willie the Lion Smith, Jonah Jones would come by and scare everybody to death, people like Buster Bailey, fine clarinetist. I did have a chance to play with Earl Father Hines in San Francisco. I had a way of lucking out when trumpet players would get sick and I'd get called. I never felt badly about being second choice because I think I would have chosen those other guys first too. There was a trumpet player named Eddie Smith working for Father Hines in San Francisco. He was very good. But he got sick for a couple weeks and I was able to play with the band, which included Darnell Howard, another New Orleans legend. I thought he was just delightful to work with, a beautiful person. I met a new Albert Nicholas in New York. I remember having dinner with him at a restaurant. He was a very elegant gentleman, loved his fine food, and he was as meticulous as his clarinet playing sounds. He was just a really fine and polished gentleman. And, of course, some of the younger people, Dick Wellstead was very close. We played in the Janus Band for a couple of years together. Chad sits. I'm not doing too well on free recall. Well, I've got a lot of questions. You name him and I've rubbed elbows. I remember Muggsy Spanier hated to play alongside the Count Rajanis Band because we always played loud and rowdy and the crowd liked it. Muggsy was growing old gracefully and played wonderful. Muggsy was a very strong early influence. I had those old Bluebird, Muggsy Spanier and the Ragtimers. I learned a lot of basic things. Of course, George Brunis was on those.
